stem: A customer-support assistant enforces four independent layers — input validation, output filtering, scoped tool permissions, and human approval on refunds above $750. To cut the compliance team's audit workload, a security lead proposes replacing all four with one fine-tuned safety classifier. Which response is correct?

opts.t: Replace the four checks with the classifier; its benchmark accuracy on refund misuse already exceeds them combined.
Keep the four layers separate; a single classifier cannot enforce tool-permission scoping or the refund approval gate itself.
Consolidate into the classifier, and add a human-approval gate on any refund it flags as high-risk.
Consolidate into the classifier, and raise its confidence threshold before it can approve a refund.

whyRight: The four layers catch different failure classes independently, and a text classifier operates at only one altitude — it cannot enforce which tools are exposed or gate a refund pending approval, so those functions must stay outside it as separate layers.

whyWrong.A: A benchmark accuracy figure describes how often the classifier judges content correctly; it says nothing about whether the classifier can enforce tool permissions or gate a refund pending approval.
whyWrong.C: Adding an approval gate on flagged refunds is real, but folding input validation, output filtering, and tool scoping into one classifier still discards the independence those layers exist to provide.
whyWrong.D: A confidence threshold changes how certain the classifier must be before acting; it does not restore the separate enforcement that tool scoping and the refund approval gate provided.

stem: A ten-step onboarding-verification pipeline tests each step at 96% accuracy alone, yet only two in three completed applications clear correctly end to end, unchanged for months at 50,000 applications a day. Select two.

opts.t: The 0.96^10 compounding math already explains the gap — no single step is failing outside its own 96% rate.
Check whether the model version backing one specific step changed sometime this week.
Add a stricter output-format instruction at the final step to catch mistakes made earlier in the chain.
Insert deterministic validation checkpoints between steps to catch and correct errors before they compound further.

whyRight: The 96% per-step rate compounds multiplicatively across ten sequential steps, so roughly one in three completions carries an uncaught error even with every step passing its own test; deterministic checkpoints between steps catch and correct errors before they propagate into later steps.

whyWrong.B: The pipeline has been unchanged for months, which the stem states directly; a version check answers a drift question the given evidence does not raise here.
whyWrong.C: A stricter instruction at the final step only screens output the earlier nine steps already produced; it does nothing to stop the compounding from reaching that point.

stem: A three-person compliance team files six regulatory disclosures a month with a national regulator; every disclosure is a binding legal filing and an error can trigger a formal inquiry. Leadership wants full accuracy without adding headcount. Which approach satisfies both?

opts.t: Score each disclosure with a confidence model, and route only the low-confidence ones to a human reviewer.
Keep full review of every disclosure, and add a fourth reviewer dedicated to the compliance team.
Route every disclosure to a compliance reviewer before filing; at six a month, full review adds no meaningful cost.
Review only disclosures above a stated exposure threshold, and let smaller filings clear without review.

whyRight: At six filings a month, reviewing every one is cheap enough that it costs nothing beyond the team's existing capacity, and because every filing is equally high-consequence, full review is also the only way to guarantee none of the six goes unreviewed.

whyWrong.A: Building a confidence model to triage six filings a month adds machinery the volume never required, and a low-confidence score is not what makes any single filing high-consequence here.
whyWrong.B: Adding a fourth reviewer achieves full coverage but adds the headcount leadership explicitly wants to avoid; the existing team can review six filings a month without it.
whyWrong.D: The stem states every disclosure is equally binding; nothing marks a smaller filing as lower-consequence, so an exposure threshold has no stated basis to divide them.

stem: A financial-services firm enforces data-residency at the network layer, blocking all outbound cross-region traffic. A vetted partner integration now needs controlled read access to specific records from one approved partner region. What should the team do?

opts.t: Add a scoped network-layer exception permitting only that partner's approved traffic, leaving the boundary control in place for everything else.
Move the residency check down to the application layer, and allow-list the partner's requests there instead.
Disable the network-layer residency control for traffic tagged as belonging to the partner integration.
Deny the integration request, since traffic to a non-approved region cannot cross the network boundary.

whyRight: The network-layer control already enforces residency correctly and deterministically; a scoped exception for one named partner's approved traffic preserves that enforcement for every other case rather than weakening the boundary itself or rebuilding the check somewhere the model or application could get wrong.

whyWrong.B: Recreating the residency check at the application layer moves enforcement somewhere the model or app logic can get wrong, when the network layer already enforces it deterministically.
whyWrong.C: Disabling the control for tagged traffic removes the boundary enforcement entirely rather than narrowing it, so any request mistakenly tagged as the partner's would cross unchecked.
whyWrong.D: The stem states the partner's region is already approved; denying the request on the premise that it is not contradicts the fact the scenario itself gives.

lessonKey: add approved boundary control else everything exception layer leaving network only partner permitting place s scoped traffic

stem: A hiring-screening model shows complaints concentrated among applicants from one demographic group. Legal proposes removing the demographic field from model input so the system cannot see protected status before the next retraining cycle. What should the team do instead?

opts.t: Reject that change; keep the field and rebuild the evaluation set stratified by subgroup instead.
Go ahead with removing the field; proxies aside, the model can no longer use protected status directly.
Raise the overall accuracy target and retrain the model until the complaint rate falls.
Recompute the same overall accuracy metric on live traffic every quarter, without changing what is measured.

whyRight: The demographic field is what makes the disparity visible in the first place; removing it destroys the measurement while leaving proxy signals like postal code or employment gaps untouched, so the team should keep the field and stratify the evaluation by subgroup instead.

whyWrong.B: Proxy variables like postal code still carry the same signal the field provided, so removing it stops the disparity from being measured without stopping it from occurring.
whyWrong.C: The complaint pattern is concentrated in one subgroup, not spread across the aggregate; raising the overall target and retraining optimizes the number that was already concealing where the failures sit.
whyWrong.D: Recomputing the same aggregate figure on a schedule is good practice generally, but it still reports one number for everyone and does not surface where the failures concentrate.

t1Clause: concentrated among applicants from one demographic group

stem: An internal tool drafts email replies for a team's private queue, with no user-facing output and no tools; the security team wants every internal tool wrapped in the same four-layer template before allocating review budget. Which control set fits this tool's risk?

opts.t: Scope the tool's actions narrowly and require human approval before any tool call executes.
Add detailed logging of every draft so the team can review usage patterns afterward.
Add a system-prompt instruction asking the model to flag any draft it is unsure about.
Keep input validation and an output schema check; skip tool scoping and human approval, since neither applies here.

whyRight: Guardrail layers are matched to consequence: this tool has no external output and no tools for anything to scope or gate, so input validation and an output schema check are the only layers with something real to check, and adding permission scoping or human approval would cover nothing.

whyWrong.A: The stem states the tool holds no tools; there is no tool call to gate and nothing to scope, so this control has nothing to act on.
whyWrong.B: Logging records what the tool already did; it does not decide which boundary control this low-consequence tool actually needs.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction depends on the model behaving as asked; it is a tendency standing in for the deterministic check the boundary needs.

t1Clause: with no user-facing output and no tools
lessonKey: checks input output schema sufficient validation

stem: A support bot handling thousands of chats daily stopped referencing anything said two turns earlier, after the team switched to a lighter client library that trims payloads; conversations run four or five turns, and the model version is unchanged. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Confirm the application is resending the full conversation history with each request.
Increase the context window setting so more prior turns fit in each call.
Roll back to the previous model version to rule out a degraded release.
Add a system-prompt reminder telling the assistant to remember what the user said earlier.

whyRight: Losing reference to something said two turns back in a short conversation is a classic missing-history symptom, not a capacity limit; the model version is pinned and unchanged, so the first check is whether the calling application still sends the full turn history with each request.

whyWrong.B: The conversation is only four or five turns; that is far below any context limit, so the stem's own evidence rules out a capacity explanation.
whyWrong.C: The model version is stated as unchanged; chasing a version rollback discards a component that was never implicated instead of checking what actually changed.
whyWrong.D: Telling the assistant to remember does nothing if the earlier turn's text was never sent back to it; the instruction cannot act on data the request never contained.

stem: A finance team can manually audit only 5% of expense reports daily, and any report over $10,000 must be checked regardless of model confidence. The current plan audits every report at rollout, easing off as trust builds. What should replace it?

opts.t: Audit every report at rollout and reduce the audit rate as trust in the model grows.
Auto-approve confident low-value reports; send every report over $10,000 to a human regardless of confidence; audit the approved stream periodically.
Randomly audit a fixed percentage of all reports, sized to the team's daily capacity.
Let the model flag any report it says it's unsure about, and audit only those.

whyRight: Auditing everything from rollout collapses the team's capacity immediately since no stopping point is named; routing on confidence and dollar amount together lets low-value, high-confidence reports clear immediately while every high-value report still reaches a human.

whyWrong.A: Auditing everything from rollout already exceeds the stated 5% capacity, and no threshold or date is named for when the rate would ease.
whyWrong.C: A fixed sample sized to capacity is a way to monitor the auto-approved stream afterward, not a way to decide which reports skip audit in the first place.
whyWrong.D: The model's own statement of confidence is not a valid routing signal -- a fluent model can be equally confident whether it is right or wrong.

t1Clause: can manually audit only 5% of expense reports daily

stem: Security wants recent request and response traffic preserved long enough to investigate incidents after the fact, while compliance requires that regulated interaction data not be kept beyond a justified, stated purpose. Which retention approach satisfies both requirements at once?

opts.t: Retain only a decision trace (versions, thresholds, outcome) for every interaction, and discard the raw traffic.
Delete all request and response logs immediately after each interaction completes.
Keep a bounded window of traffic, de-identified, under a stated investigation purpose and duration.
Retain all traffic indefinitely, restricted to the security team through role-based permissions.

whyRight: A bounded window with a stated investigation purpose and de-identification lets the security team trace recent incidents while capping how long regulated traffic exists, satisfying the retention limit and the operational need with a single design choice rather than trading one for the other.

whyWrong.A: A decision trace records what a rule concluded, not the underlying interaction content; an incident investigation needs the actual traffic, which this discards entirely.
whyWrong.B: Deleting immediately removes anything to investigate after the fact, satisfying the retention limit only by defeating the stated investigative need entirely.
whyWrong.D: Indefinite retention with access controls still leaves regulated traffic stored with no bounded duration or purpose; access control does not shrink the retention exposure.

t1Clause: Security wants recent request and response traffic preserved long enough to investigate incidents after the fact
lessonKey: 30 bounded coded days de e g identified purpose window
